title: LCA of a Cotton T-Shirt: From Fibre to End-of-Life
sub: A cradle-to-grave assessment of a 180 g cotton T-shirt worn 50 times, comparing conventional, organic and recycled-cotton blend fibres and a longer-life use scenario.
pdf: Case 02 — LCA of a Cotton T-Shirt: Executive Summary
fu: One cotton T-shirt (180 g, size M) worn 50 times and washed 25 times by a consumer in Germany
ref: 180 g finished garment, requiring 620 g seed cotton, 230 g lint, 205 g yarn and 200 g dyed fabric; 25 washes at 40 °C and 10 tumble-dry cycles
boundary: Cradle-to-grave: cotton cultivation, ginning, spinning, knitting, wet processing, cut-make-trim, distribution and retail, consumer washing and drying, collection, reuse and disposal
geo: Cotton grown in India; spinning, knitting, dyeing and sewing in Bangladesh; retail, use and end-of-life in Germany
time: 2024–2026 technology and grid mixes; GWP100 (IPCC AR6)
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100 for climate change; AWARE for water scarcity; ReCiPe 2016 land occupation
alloc: Cotton lint vs cottonseed allocated economically (≈85% to lint); recycled cotton fibre enters burden-free (cut-off) and carries only collection and mechanical recycling
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (labels, sewing thread, hangers) with cumulative exclusions <5%
dq: Secondary data from textile LCA studies and databases; Bangladeshi grid factors; consumer behaviour from European surveys. Overall data quality Medium; Low for dyeing chemicals
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges reported by Textile Exchange, the PEF apparel pilot, ecoinvent and published cotton T-shirt LCAs.
loop: Circular loop: resale and reuse, repair, and fibre-to-fibre recycling of post-consumer textiles
exec:
This case study assesses a 180 g cotton T-shirt worn 50 times, from cotton field to end-of-life. Textiles are a priority sector under the EU Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles, extended producer responsibility for textiles is being introduced, and separate collection of textile waste has been mandatory in EU Member States since 2025.
The illustrative baseline result is 6.8 kg CO2e and about 1,350 litres of water consumed per T-shirt. Wet processing (dyeing and finishing) on a coal-heavy grid is the largest climate hotspot, followed by consumer washing and tumble drying, cotton cultivation and spinning. Irrigated cotton cultivation accounts for almost 90% of water consumption.
Organic cotton reduces water consumption by about 70% but changes the climate result by only about 7%. A recycled-cotton blend saves water and land but has a similar carbon footprint. The largest reduction comes from use: a garment that lasts 100 wears, is dyed with renewable energy and is line-dried cuts the climate impact per 50 wears by almost 60%.
Recommendations focus on durability, renewable energy at wet-processing suppliers and consumer care. For CSRD, results support ESRS E1 (Scope 3), E3 (water in stressed basins), E5 (product durability and textile waste) and S2 (garment and cotton workers).
overview:
A basic cotton jersey T-shirt is one of the highest-volume garments sold worldwide. Its supply chain spans cotton farms, ginning mills, spinners, knitters, dye houses and garment factories, often in different countries, before reaching European retailers.
The purpose of this LCA is to understand which life-cycle stages drive environmental impacts, how fibre choices compare, and how much design for durability and consumer care can change the result.
goal: The goal is to support a fashion retailer's product design, fibre sourcing and circular-business decisions by quantifying the life-cycle impacts of a basic T-shirt and comparing fibre and use scenarios. The audience is design, sourcing and sustainability teams. Results are not intended for public comparative claims or product labelling.

stages.what: Cotton is grown, irrigated, fertilised and harvested; seed cotton is delivered to gins.
stages.in: Land, irrigation water, N fertiliser, pesticides, diesel
stages.ew: Irrigation 1,180 L per T-shirt; diesel for tractors and pumps
stages.em: N2O from fertiliser; CO2 from diesel and pumping
stages.so: Forced-labour risk in some origins; pesticide exposure of farm workers
stages.as: Indian conventional cotton, 50% irrigated; yield 500 kg lint/ha

stages.what: Lint is separated from seed, cleaned, carded and ring-spun into yarn.
stages.ew: ≈2.3 kWh per T-shirt, mainly in spinning
stages.wa: Spinning waste (often recycled into lower-grade yarn)
stages.so: Long working hours in spinning mills
stages.as: Indian grid; ring spinning, Ne 30 yarn

stages.what: Yarn is knitted into single-jersey fabric on circular knitting machines.
Fabric is scoured, bleached, dyed with reactive dyes, washed and finished.
stages.in: Fabric, water, heat from gas or coal boilers, dyes, salts, auxiliaries
stages.em: CO2 from boilers; wastewater with dyes and salts
stages.so: Chemical exposure; wastewater discharge affecting communities
stages.as: Gas and coal boilers; effluent treatment plant assumed operating

stages.what: Fabric is cut, sewn, labelled, inspected and packed.
stages.so: Low wages, freedom-of-association and building-safety risks

stages.what: Garments are shipped to Europe, distributed and sold in stores and online.
stages.in: Heavy fuel oil, diesel, store energy, packaging
stages.ew: Store energy allocated by floor space
stages.tr: Chittagong–Hamburg 16,000 km by sea; 500 km by truck

stages.what: The consumer washes the T-shirt 25 times at 40 °C and tumble-dries it 10 times; no ironing.
stages.ew: ≈2.8 kWh electricity and 52 L water over the life
stages.em: CO2 from electricity; detergent to wastewater
stages.as: Shared machine loads; German grid 0.38 kg CO2e/kWh

stages.what: 25% of garments are collected for reuse or recycling; the remainder go to residual waste and are incinerated.
stages.tr: Collection 50 km; export of second-hand clothing excluded
stages.so: Second-hand exports can create waste burdens in importing countries
stages.as: Cut-off: reuse benefits not credited to this product

hot.why: Steam from coal and gas boilers makes dyeing and finishing the largest single climate contributor (≈24%) and a major source of chemical and wastewater pressure.
Irrigated cotton accounts for almost 90% of water consumption, much of it in basins with high water scarcity.
Tumble drying alone uses more electricity than washing. Use accounts for about a quarter of the climate result and depends entirely on consumer behaviour.
Conventional cotton relies on synthetic nitrogen and pesticides, contributing to N2O emissions, eutrophication and ecotoxicity.
Every production burden is divided by the number of wears. A garment discarded after 20 wears has more than double the impact per wear of one used 50 times.

desc: Indian conventional cotton; coal/gas steam; 50 wears; tumble-dried 10 times
Certified organic cotton, rain-fed share higher; no synthetic fertiliser; lower yield
50% mechanically recycled post-industrial cotton, 50% conventional; shorter fibres require similar spinning energy
Organic cotton, renewable heat and power at dye house, garment lasts 100 wears (impacts shown per 50 wears), always line-dried

sens.t: Sensitivity: number of wears before disposal
sens.xl: Number of wears in the garment's life
sens.note: Lifetime (number of wears) is the most influential parameter because production burdens are spread over the garment's use. Use-phase energy is held per wear.
sens.interp: Doubling wears from 50 to 100 cuts impact per wear by about 40%, more than any fibre switch tested. Durability and reuse should be central to circular design.

ci.stage: Dyeing and finishing is the largest stage, followed by consumer use and cotton cultivation. Impacts are spread across several countries and suppliers.
ci.stage_e: Energy demand is dominated by wet processing and consumer use (washing and tumble drying).
ci.stage_w: Cotton irrigation dominates water consumption; wet processing is a distant second.
ci.donut: More than 70% of the climate result arises in the supply chain before the garment reaches the store, and about a quarter in consumer use.
ci.sankey: Only about 30% of the seed cotton mass ends up in the T-shirt. At end-of-life, two thirds of garments are still incinerated with residual waste.
ci.heat: Cultivation is a hotspot for water, land and eutrophication; dyeing for climate, energy and toxicity; use for climate and energy.
ci.scen: Fibre changes affect mainly the cultivation stage. Durability and use behaviour reduce every stage per functional unit.
ci.radar: Organic cotton has the best water profile but uses more land; recycled blend has the best land result; the durable scenario performs best overall.
ci.wf: Doubling lifetime is the largest single lever; renewable heat at wet-processing suppliers and line drying follow.

interp.m: A T-shirt's climate footprint comes from energy in wet processing and consumer use, while its water footprint comes from irrigated cotton. Fibre choice matters most for water and land, not for carbon.
interp.a: Number of wears; energy sources at the dye house; irrigation share of cotton; tumble-drying frequency; allocation between lint and cottonseed.
interp.u: Supplier energy mixes vary widely; water consumption per kg cotton varies by an order of magnitude between regions; consumer behaviour is uncertain.
interp.can: Durability and supplier energy are the largest climate levers; organic and recycled cotton reduce water use; tumble drying is a significant consumer-phase hotspot.
interp.cannot: The study cannot rank brands, quantify microfibre release (cotton is not a plastic fibre, but blends with polyester would be), or measure social impacts such as wages.
interp.d: Supplier selection for wet processing, durability specifications, fibre strategy for water-stressed regions, care-label guidance, take-back and resale programmes.

recs: Specify durability (pilling, seam strength, colour fastness) and design for repair and resale; avoid blends that block recycling.
Prioritise dye houses with renewable steam and verified effluent treatment; source cotton from lower water-stress regions or organic and recycled programmes.
Switch boilers from coal to biomass, electrification or solar thermal; adopt low-liquor-ratio dyeing and heat recovery.
Offer take-back, repair and resale; communicate care guidance (wash cold, line-dry) without overstating benefits.
Improve sorting for reuse and fibre-to-fibre recycling; ensure exports of used textiles meet quality criteria.
Report Scope 3 Category 1 by supplier tier; track water use in stressed basins and the share of durable and recycled products.
Implement textile extended producer responsibility with eco-modulated fees rewarding durability; support recycling infrastructure.

take: For a T-shirt, how long it is worn matters more than which cotton it is made from; fibre choice mainly changes water and land, while durability and supplier energy change the carbon result.
biz: Build durability and resale into the product range, require renewable steam and verified effluent treatment from wet-processing suppliers, and use organic or recycled cotton to manage water risk rather than as a carbon claim.
assume: 50 wears and 25 washes; 40% of washes tumble-dried; Indian cotton 50% irrigated; coal and gas steam at the dye house; sea freight only; reuse benefits not credited (cut-off). Social impacts and microfibre release are discussed qualitatively only.
